title: Serengeti Field Notebook
time: 25–35 min · selected stations
question: Why did people protect the Serengeti, and how did they decide what to protect?
plan: Write two different investigation questions.
Compare two months on the map. Pin or note evidence from two stations.
Use two pieces of evidence to explain a boundary decision. Write one new question.
turnIn: Preview report: turn in your explanation, station evidence, and new question.
fallback: If a video is blocked, use the history and written station exhibits.

title: Migration Map Explorer
time: 40–50 min · selected questions
question: What might explain why wildebeest move through the Serengeti during the year?
plan: Compare two months on the map. Pause and save a note about each month.
In Investigate evidence, compare the same anthrax measure across June or July groups.
Explain what the evidence supports. Cite the month, group, and measure.
turnIn: Turn in a draft report with the two saved observations and an evidence-based explanation.
fallback: If the interview is blocked, use the field health cards and their matching graph.

title: Carrying Capacity
time: 45–55 min · grass model
question: How does grass availability affect the number of wildebeest the model can support?
plan: Save a prediction and run the baseline grass model.
Change only grass availability. Record a comparison and examine rounds 7–12.
Use counts from both runs to answer the five core explanation prompts.
turnIn: Turn in the report with both model runs and your core explanations.
fallback: Use a projected model run and copy its round counts into a comparison table.

title: Serengeti Board Game
time: 45–60 min · includes analysis
question: How do migration and predator–prey encounters change the modeled herd?
plan: Choose solo or numbered group roles. Review the dice example before the first hunt.
Play from winter through fall. Keep track of events and changes in the record.
Choose a numbered event or hunt. Use it to explain one herd change and a model limit.
turnIn: Turn in the board’s report with the event number and your analysis. Group reports need no names.
fallback: Use the written How to play and dice example if the walkthrough video is blocked.

title: Serengeti Ripple Effects
time: 15–20 min · after the board game
question: Why might migration matter to organisms that never migrate?
plan: Build and check all six connections in the local influence web.
Predict a change in dung beetle activity. Record both visit scenarios.
Compare the same model step, trace two links, and explain one limit.
turnIn: Turn in your report with both runs and your explanation of the ripple effect.
fallback: If devices are limited, compare both scenarios from a shared or projected run.

title: Burning Fuels: What Burns and Why
time: About 40 min
question: What can simulated burning tell us about why peat can fuel a fire?
plan: Predict the temperature change. Weigh each fuel and take its starting temperature.
Simulate all five burns. Reweigh and reread temperature to save each run.
Compare mass loss, temperature change, and indicator color. Explain one fair-test limit.
turnIn: Turn in the report with recorded burns and an evidence-based explanation.
fallback: If the simulation will not run, analyze teacher-provided readings. Do not burn fuels at home.

title: Fires: Peat, Decomposition & Earth’s Tilt
time: About 60 min total · can split
question: How could temperature and light affect how much peat builds up?
plan: Lesson 3: predict and compare yeast foam over time at different temperatures.
Lesson 5: compare indicator readings from tubes under different light conditions.
Use a reading from each test to explain how peat formed or remained.
turnIn: Turn in evidence from both tests and your explanation, or a draft for one assigned test.
fallback: Use the labeled class example to discuss an unavailable comparison. Mark it as example data.

title: Peat Bog Carbon Lab
time: 45–60 min · trial comparison
question: What changes whether a modeled Arctic peat bog stores or releases carbon?
plan: Choose a starting scenario and record a baseline trial.
Change one setting and save a labeled trial. Keep other settings fixed.
Use two graph values to compare process rates and explain the net carbon result.
turnIn: Turn in the report with your matched trials and the Test one variable response.
fallback: Use a projected or printed trial table and label its readings as simulated.

title: Carbon Atom Journey
time: 30–40 min · dice journey
question: Where can one carbon atom go, and how is its movement different from energy transfer?
plan: Record at least ten rolls, including stays.
Review any required reference cards, then finish the Journey.
Use two recorded turns in Make sense. Distinguish what moved from what happened to energy.
turnIn: Turn in the report with your journal and Make sense responses. Budget is optional unless assigned.
fallback: Use the printed Lesson 9 station cards and a paper journal if the model is unavailable.

title: Cancer Rates Data Dive
question: What do cancer diagnosis and death rates tell us, and what do they leave out?
plan: Save a prediction. Open the Evidence Folder, save observations for A–C, and complete the checks for D–F.
Save a follow-up question. Choose a dataset that answers it and pin two groups with reported values.
In Explain, use both values and units to support a claim. Name one limit and select Finish investigation.
turnIn: Submit your finished activity report with the six exhibits, question, pinned comparison, claim, and limitation. Use population data only; no personal or family health information.
fallback: If the chart is hard to read, use its data table. If the site is unavailable, use the lesson figures and a teacher-provided table to record a comparison and limitation on paper.

title: Cancer Screening Design Lab
lesson: Engineering extension after the Data Dive
question: How could a clinic network improve access to needed care within its budget?
plan: Read the three fictional cases and run the hospital plan. Note each person’s care needs, costs, and travel time.
Move the ultrasound machine and trained operator together. Run a redesign and check the same three cases in both plans.
In Recommend a plan, use patient and clinic costs as evidence. Name who could still miss care and finish.
turnIn: Submit the finished report with both plans, all three checked comparisons, and your recommendation. A winning design is not required.
fallback: Without a device, use a teacher-provided district results table and cost sheets. Compare the same cases on paper. The fictional credits and imaging outcomes are not medical advice.

title: Cell Cycle & Cancer
time: About 40 min for the short route; 2 periods for the full activity
question: How does a longer time to divide change the number of opportunities to copy DNA?
plan: Skip the Cell-cycle game for this short route. In Growth model, write a prediction and run skin cells to age 50 at average body size.
Run a second set to age 70 with the same tissue and body size. Both sets have three trials.
In Analyze, answer Q1, Q2, and Q4a with your results. Select one model limit, then open Wrap up.
turnIn: Submit your report with both sets and the assigned answers and limit. An In progress report is expected for this short route.
fallback: Use a teacher-provided pair of three-trial sets. Compare means and variation on paper. Simulated counts are not individual cancer risks.

title: DNA Workshop: Build, Copy, Decode
question: How do copying DNA, making RNA, and building an amino acid chain differ?
plan: Build a nucleotide from a phosphate, a sugar, and a base. Use the pairing key to build the complementary DNA.
Copy DNA and identify an original strand in each result. Make RNA using one DNA strand as the template.
Decode the fictional RNA message with the codon key. Complete the final product sort.
turnIn: Show your completed final sort or submit the activity report if assigned. Written observations are optional.
fallback: If dragging is difficult, select a piece and then its slot by touch or keyboard. Without a device, use a teacher-provided fictional sequence and printed pairing and codon keys.

title: DNA Copying, p53 & Gene Expression
time: 60–75 min total or 2 sessions by lesson
question: How can a DNA copying error change the information a cell passes on?
plan: Open DNA fork and record the correctly paired letters and mismatches on both strands before using the p53 model.
Try version a, replace any missing letters, and record both strands again. Use the before-and-after counts to explain the result.
In Making sense and Explanation, distinguish a copying error from a lasting mutation. Save your work for the next session.
turnIn: Submit your Lesson 5 report as a draft. In Lesson 6, record expression runs for strands A, B, and C and complete the remaining responses for the finished report.
fallback: Use teacher-provided before-and-after fork evidence to write an explanation. The model simplifies DNA repair; its p53 piece does not show what the protein does directly in a cell.

title: Inheritance, Environment & Cancer Risk
time: 1 period for Lesson 9 only; 60–80 min for both lessons
question: What can a controlled UV model show that a pattern across places cannot?
plan: Start at Environment for Lesson 9 only. Compare the skin-cancer graphs and note one pattern and one uncertainty.
In Plan a test, choose one variable to change and a result to measure. Run a controlled comparison in Virtual yeast.
Use recorded colony counts for a claim and explanation. In Wrap up, distinguish simulated yeast survival from cancer risk in people.
turnIn: Submit the Lesson 9 report with your testable question, modeled results, evidence-based claim, and wrap-up. The family activities are not required for this route.
fallback: Use teacher-provided lesson graphs and virtual results without any real exposure experiment. Compare the graph pattern and classroom model on paper. No family health information is needed.

title: Hawksbeard Wind Lab
time: 20–30 min digitally; allow extra time for the published study.
question: How does the landing surface affect which hawksbeard seeds reach soil in a field and a city?
plan: Predict where feathery and nonfeathery seeds will land before starting a release.
Release all five matched plant pairs. Compare soil landings in the field and city.
Revisit your prediction, then compare the nonfeathery share of soil landings. Name both denominators and explain a limit.
turnIn: Use Preview report to save your prediction, paired trial data, and written comparison and explanation.
fallback: Use the physical seed-dispersal test or teacher-provided paired landing counts. On paper, compute both fractions and explain what a soil landing does not show.

title: Rat Generations
time: 30–40 min for the model and explanation; reading discussion is separate.
question: How can selection change which inherited alleles become more common over generations?
plan: Save a prediction. Move each assigned parent pair to its nest and complete its Punnett square.
Follow the colony through Gen 5. Compare births with survivors in Gen 3 and Gen 4.
Use a count and a percentage to explain what changed. Keep colony size, trait percentage, and allele frequency separate.
turnIn: Save your generation record, quick check, and explanations through Preview report.
fallback: Use the Lesson 3 bead model and paper Punnett squares. Record births and survivors, then make the same comparison from your table.

title: Junco Investigation
time: 25–35 min for the digital investigation and partner discussion.
question: What does shared aviary care help explain about differences between city and mountain juncos?
plan: Compare flight distances for one matching field situation. Write a note naming both populations.
Identify the matched aviary conditions. Save an exploration prediction and reveal the results.
Read one CORT scatterplot point. Explain the aviary outcome with evidence from two parts and name a limit.
turnIn: Save your field note, aviary prediction, evidence-based explanation, and limit or next question through Preview report.
fallback: Use printed field, aviary, and CORT graphs from Lesson 4. Write the same prediction, evidence comparison, and limitation on paper.

title: Wildlife Corridor Lab
time: 25–35 min for the digital companion; keep the original reading and discussion.
question: How could a road crossing change the movement of inherited alleles between separated populations?
plan: Compare earlier and recent Florida panther range maps. Predict which modeled setup will make allele counts more similar.
Run the connected habitat and no-crossing road for eight generations. Place a crossing and rerun from the same start.
Inspect one offspring’s two inherited copies. Compare the road runs using A-copy counts and explain what the model cannot show.
turnIn: Choose Finish investigation, then save your matched runs and evidence-based explanation through Preview report.
fallback: Provide a printed matched set of the three model runs. Have students trace one inheritance example with allele cards and compare the A-copy gaps on paper.

title: Three Bears in Wapusk
time: 25–35 min of digital work across the lesson; keep the original discussions and models.
question: What do different kinds of evidence tell us about bears in changing Arctic habitats?
plan: Switch seasons in the Wapusk map and compare the schematic with the original sighting maps. Record a seasonal pattern.
Compare evidence at two scales. Investigate one assigned region and separate what its evidence shows from what remains unknown.
Draw or describe two initial models, one for seasonal ice and one for persistent ice. Write one Driving Question Board question.
turnIn: Save your observations, regional evidence, two initial models, and question through Preview report.
fallback: Use the original sighting maps, Data Exploration slides, Scale Organizer, and regional handouts or transcript. Record both models on paper.

title: Bear Thermoregulation Lab
time: 25–35 min digitally; collecting human readings and class discussion need separate time.
question: Could overheating help explain why a polar bear might give up a food source?
plan: Predict what happens at a shared food source. Revisit the prediction using a field observation.
Compare breaks at two treadmill speeds and read the core-temperature graph. Analyze human surface readings or the labeled practice table.
Sort all six matter and energy cards. Explain the overheating idea using field and lab evidence, then propose a field test.
turnIn: Save your field and treadmill comparisons, temperature analysis, card placements, and explanation through Preview report.
fallback: Use the printed field evidence, treadmill table, and temperature graph. Provide the labeled practice readings and sort paper matter and energy cards.

title: Bear Ancestry Lab
time: 25–35 min digitally; specimen stations and partner discussion are separate.
question: Which two of the three bears share the most recent common ancestor, and what evidence supports that?
plan: Compare the trait stations. Save a first guess about the closest pair using an observed trait.
Compare DNA alignments for the three pairs. Record differences in the comparison log.
Build and check a tree. Explain one branch point and whether the trait and DNA evidence changed your first guess.
turnIn: Save your trait observation, DNA comparison log, tree, and revised explanation through Preview report.
fallback: Use available specimens or printed trait stations, the Bear Traits Organizer, and a printed alignment. Count differences and sketch the tree on paper.

title: Ice Age Bear Speciation Explorer
time: 30–40 min digitally; if split across periods, pause after the first argument.
question: How might changing ice and inherited traits have contributed to the separation of bear lineages?
plan: Choose a climate cycle, place bears in both phases, and check generation estimates. Save a first argument.
Pin one fossil of each bear type and compare their ages and sites. Read all three gene cards and test a bear in each habitat.
Revise your argument using climate, fossil, and genetic evidence. Name what remains uncertain and write one next question.
turnIn: Finish the investigation and save both arguments, fossil pins, trait matches, and conclusion check through Preview report.
fallback: Use the Glacial and Interglacial Periods, Bear Fossils Map, and Genetic Bear Data handouts. Save the initial argument on paper before introducing the fossil and trait evidence.

title: Arctic Bear Futures & Hybridization
time: 25–35 min digitally plus class discussion; use after the Lesson 5 model revision.
question: What can sea-ice projections, a real bear family, and a simulation tell us about possible futures for hybrids?
plan: Pin a future year. Compare lower- and higher-emissions September sea-ice area and write a prediction.
Visit both islands and trace one first-generation hybrid and one backcross. Separate family evidence from encounter counts.
Record ten simulated matings. Use a trait count to explain one habitat trade-off and state what the simulation cannot predict.
turnIn: Finish the investigation and save the climate comparison, family evidence, mating record, and claim through Preview report.
fallback: Use the printed Future Predictions figure and pedigree. Use four coin flips per mating for ten matings, then tally traits and write the claim on paper.
